label: Uruk around 3200 BC

location.coordinateMeaning: An archaeological-site centre used to test the broad Late Uruk city, not a claim that one excavated building occupied the exact pin.

temporal.supportedResolution: Broad Late Uruk horizon around 3200 BC.
temporal.precisionBoundary: The sources do not establish an exact year, street, ruler, population count, season, or named event.

habitation.evidence: Uruk was the largest settlement in southern Mesopotamia and a true city around 3200 BC, with monumental and extensive urban functions.
habitation.qualification: Dense is a spatial rendering obligation for a major city, not a sourced headcount for one exact frame.

viewpoint.support: An active compact urban exterior with packed earth or mudbrick material under the optic.
invalidAlternatives: a view from an unsupported sanctuary interior

visibleGroundTruth.claim: Around 3200 BC Uruk was a true city and possibly the world's largest settlement.
visibleGroundTruth.visualConsequence: Continuous built surroundings and active people at several depths should make the city hard to see past.

visibleGroundTruth.claim: Monumental buildings used mudbrick and some carried painted clay-cone mosaics.
visibleGroundTruth.visualConsequence: Mudbrick dominates; cone mosaics can date selected monumental surfaces without decorating every wall.

visibleGroundTruth.claim: Uruk developed on the margin of a freshwater-marsh deltaic landscape rather than today's dry plain.
visibleGroundTruth.visualConsequence: Water, wet ground, channels, reeds, or marsh-edge distance should distinguish the living city from its modern ruins.

visibleGroundTruth.claim: Administrative clay records and proto-writing belong to the period.
visibleGroundTruth.visualConsequence: Clay tablets and managed goods are possible small-scale markers, not mandatory giant symbols.

obligations: Make Uruk a socially and materially dense working city.
Use mudbrick as the architectural ground truth.
Place activity and bodies at several distances rather than isolating one artifact.
Retain the freshwater-marsh or managed-water relation without turning the city into open swamp.
Reserve painted cone mosaics for appropriate monumental surfaces.
oracleOnlyContradictions: Today's arid eroded ruins are not the 3200 BC land state.
Cone mosaics are not universal wall treatment.
A tablet corpus does not license readable modern-looking text in the image.
Exact population, street plan, clothing distribution, and channel course remain uncertain.

sources.title: The Metropolitan Museum of Art - Uruk: The First City
UNESCO World Heritage - Ahwar and the relict Mesopotamian cities
Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative - Uruk III tablet

uncertainty: Exact local channel course and street plan.
Ordinary domestic architecture and dress in one frame.
Population total and density at the exact pin.
Visibility of any named temple or wall around 3200 BC.

review.notes: The around-3200 BC city, mudbrick, cone-mosaic, administrative, and marsh-margin claims are source-checked. Exact site-phase rendering remains bounded.
